title.en: The Tao That Can Be Trodden: The Nameless Beginning (Tao Te Ching 1)
title.zh: 道可道，非常道（道德經第一章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 1

summary.en: The opening cosmogony of the classic of the Way: the Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao; the Nameless is the origin of Heaven and Earth; the Named is the mother of all things — both secrets, doubly profound, the door from which issued the secret of the way of life.
summary.zh: 道可道，非常道；名可名，非常名。無名，天地之始；有名，萬物之母。玄之又玄，眾妙之門。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The Tao which can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao; the name which can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name. 2. (Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of Heaven and Earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.

3. Always without desire we must be found, if its deep mystery we would sound; and if ever we are need desire, its outer fringe is all that we shall see. 4. Under these two aspects, it is really the same; but as development takes place, it receives the different designations. 5. Together we may call them the Mystery. 6. Where the Mystery is the deepest is the gate of all that is subtle and wonderful.

title.en: The Honoured Ancestor of All Things (Tao Te Ching 4)
title.zh: 吾不知誰之子，象帝之先（道德經第四章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 4

summary.en: The Tao is like the emptiness of a vessel, deep and unfathomable, as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of all things — I do not know whose son it is: it might appear to have been before God (the Lord of Heaven).
summary.zh: 道沖而用之，或不盈；淵兮似萬物之宗——吾不知誰之子，象帝之先。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel; and in our employment of it we must be on our guard against all fulness. How deep and unfathomable it is, as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of all things!

2. We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of things; we should attemper our brightness, and bring ourselves into agreement with the obscurity of others. How pure and still the Tao is, as if it would ever so continue! 3. I do not know whose son it is. It might appear to have been before God.

title.en: Straw Dogs and the Bellows of Heaven and Earth (Tao Te Ching 5)
title.zh: 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗（道德經第五章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 5

summary.en: Heaven and earth do not act from any wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with — and the space between heaven and earth is like a bellows: 'tis emptied, yet it loses not its power; 'tis moved again, and sends forth air the more.
summary.zh: 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗；聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗。天地之間，其猶橐籥乎——虛而不屈，動而愈出。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; the straw dog (ch'u-kou) is the funeral-sacrifice image echoed in Zhuangzi's ch. 14. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: 1. Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with. The sages do not act from (any wish to be) benevolent; they deal with the people as the dogs of grass are dealt with.

2. May not the space between heaven and earth be compared to a bellows? 'Tis emptied, yet it loses not its power; 'Tis moved again, and sends forth air the more. Much speech to swift exhaustion lead we see; Your inner being guard, and keep it free.

title.en: The Valley Spirit Dies Not: The Mystery of the Female (Tao Te Ching 6)
title.zh: 谷神不死，是謂玄牝（道德經第六章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 6

summary.en: The valley spirit dies not, aye the same; the female mystery thus do we name. Its gate, from which at first they issued forth, is called the root from which grew heaven and earth.
summary.zh: 谷神不死，是謂玄牝；玄牝之門，是謂天地根。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; the 'mysterious female' (hsüan-p'in) became a core inner-alchemy image. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: The valley spirit dies not, aye the same; The female mystery thus do we name. Its gate, from which at first they issued forth, Is called the root from which grew heaven and earth. Long and unbroken does its power remain, Used gently, and without the touch of pain.

title.en: The Thirty Spokes and the Empty Nave (Tao Te Ching 11)
title.zh: 三十輻共一轂（道德經第十一章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 11

summary.en: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; clay is fashioned into vessels; doors and windows are cut out to form an apartment — but it is on the empty space that their use depends. What has positive existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for actual usefulness.
summary.zh: 三十輻共一轂，當其無，有車之用；埏埴以為器，當其無，有器之用——故有之以為利，無之以為用。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends. The door and windows are cut out (from the walls) to form an apartment; but it is on the empty space (within), that its use depends. Therefore, what has a (positive) existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has not that for (actual) usefulness.

title.en: The Equable, the Inaudible, and the Subtle: The Form of the Formless (Tao Te Ching 14)
title.zh: 視之不見名曰夷（道德經第十四章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 14

summary.en: We look at it and do not see it, and name it the Equable; we listen and do not hear it, the Inaudible; we try to grasp it and do not get hold of it, the Subtle. These three blended obtain The One — we meet it and do not see its Front; we follow it and do not see its Back. When we can lay hold of the Tao of old to direct the things of the present day, this is called unwinding the clue of Tao.
summary.zh: 視之不見名曰夷，聽之不聞名曰希，摶之不得名曰微——迎之不見其首，隨之不見其後；執古之道，以御今之有。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. We look at it, and we do not see it, and we name it 'the Equable.' We listen to it, and we do not hear it, and we name it 'the Inaudible.' We try to grasp it, and do not get hold of it, and we name it 'the Subtle.' With these three qualities, it cannot be made the subject of description; and hence we blend them together and obtain The One.

2. Its upper part is not bright, and its lower part is not obscure. Ceaseless in its action, it yet cannot be named, and then it again returns and becomes nothing. This is called the Form of the Formless, and the Semblance of the Invisible; this is called the Fleeting and Indeterminable.

3. We meet it and do not see its Front; we follow it, and do not see its Back. When we can lay hold of the Tao of old to direct the things of the present day, and are able to know it as it was of old in the beginning, this is called (unwinding) the clue of Tao.

title.en: Return to the Root: The Unchanging Rule (Tao Te Ching 16)
title.zh: 致虛極，守靜篤（道德經第十六章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 16

summary.en: All things alike go through their processes of activity, and then we see them return to their original state; when things in the vegetable world have displayed their luxuriant growth, each of them returns to its root — the regular, unchanging rule whose knowledge is intelligence; he who is king-like goes on to be heaven-like, and possessed of the Tao he endures long.
summary.zh: 致虛極，守靜篤；萬物並作，吾以觀其復——夫物芸芸，各復歸其根；歸根曰靜，是謂復命。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree, and that of stillness guarded with unwearying vigour. All things alike go through their processes of activity, and (then) we see them return (to their original state). When things (in the vegetable world) have displayed their luxuriant growth, we see each of them return to its root. This returning to their root is what we call the state of stillness; and that stillness may be called a reporting that they have fulfilled their appointed end.

2. The report of that fulfilment is the regular, unchanging rule. To know that unchanging rule is to be intelligent; not to know it leads to wild movements and evil issues. The knowledge of that unchanging rule produces a (grand) capacity and forbearance, and that capacity and forbearance lead to a community (of feeling with all things). From this community of feeling comes a kingliness of character; and he who is king-like goes on to be heaven-like. In that likeness to heaven he possesses the Tao. Possessed of the Tao, he endures long; and to the end of his bodily life, is exempt from all danger of decay.

title.en: I Alone Am Different: Carried About as on the Sea (Tao Te Ching 20)
title.zh: 絕學無憂，眾人熙熙（道德經第二十章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 20

summary.en: The multitude look satisfied, as if enjoying a full banquet, as if mounted on a tower in spring; I alone seem listless and still, like an infant which has not yet smiled, carried about as on the sea, drifting as if I had nowhere to rest — I alone am different from other men, but I value the nursing-mother, the Tao.
summary.zh: 眾人熙熙，如享太牢，如春登臺；我獨泊兮其未兆，如嬰兒之未孩——乘乘兮若無所歸。我獨異於人，而貴食母。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The multitude of men look satisfied and pleased; as if enjoying a full banquet, as if mounted on a tower in spring. I alone seem listless and still, my desires having as yet given no indication of their presence. I am like an infant which has not yet smiled. I look dejected and forlorn, as if I had no home to go to.

Ordinary men look bright and intelligent, while I alone seem to be benighted. They look full of discrimination, while I alone am dull and confused. I seem to be carried about as on the sea, drifting as if I had nowhere to rest. All men have their spheres of action, while I alone seem dull and incapable, like a rude borderer. (Thus) I alone am different from other men, but I value the nursing-mother (the Tao).

title.en: The Grandest Forms of Active Force Come from the Tao (Tao Te Ching 21)
title.zh: 孔德之容，惟道是從（道德經第二十一章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 21

summary.en: The grandest forms of active force from Tao come, their only source — eluding sight, eluding touch, the forms of things all in it crouch; profound it is, dark and obscure; things' essences all there endure. Now it is so; 'twas so of old. Its name — what passes not away.
summary.zh: 孔德之容，惟道是從；道之為物，惟恍惟惚——窈兮冥兮，其中有精；其精甚真，其中有信。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: The grandest forms of active force From Tao come, their only source. Who can of Tao the nature tell? Our sight it flies, our touch as well. Eluding sight, eluding touch, The forms of things all in it crouch; Eluding touch, eluding sight, There are their semblances, all right. Profound it is, dark and obscure; Things' essences all there endure. Those essences the truth enfold Of what, when seen, shall then be told. Now it is so; 'twas so of old. Its name--what passes not away; So, in their beautiful array, Things form and never know decay.

title.en: The Things Which from of Old Have Got the One (Tao Te Ching 39)
title.zh: 昔之得一者：天得一以清（道德經第三十九章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 39

summary.en: The things which from of old have got the One: heaven which by it is bright and pure, earth rendered firm and sure, spirits with powers by it supplied, valleys kept full throughout their void, all creatures which through it do live, princes and kings who from it get the model which to all they give. If heaven were not thus pure, it soon would rend.
summary.zh: 昔之得一者：天得一以清，地得一以寧，神得一以靈，谷得一以盈，萬物得一以生，侯王得一以為天下正——天無以清將恐裂。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The things which from of old have got the One (the Tao) are-- Heaven which by it is bright and pure; Earth rendered thereby firm and sure; Spirits with powers by it supplied; Valleys kept full throughout their void All creatures which through it do live Princes and kings who from it get The model which to all they give.

2. If heaven were not thus pure, it soon would rend; If earth were not thus sure, 'twould break and bend; Without these powers, the spirits soon would fail; If not so filled, the drought would parch each vale; Without that life, creatures would pass away; Princes and kings, without that moral sway, However grand and high, would all decay.

title.en: The Movement of the Tao by Contraries Proceeds (Tao Te Ching 40)
title.zh: 反者道之動（道德經第四十章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 40

summary.en: The movement of the Tao by contraries proceeds; and weakness marks the course of Tao's mighty deeds. All things under heaven sprang from It as existing (and named); that existence sprang from It as non-existent (and not named).
summary.zh: 反者道之動，弱者道之用；天下萬物生於有，有生於無。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. The movement of the Tao By contraries proceeds; And weakness marks the course Of Tao's mighty deeds. 2. All things under heaven sprang from It as existing (and named); that existence sprang from It as non-existent (and not named).

title.en: The Three Ministers of Life and the Three Ministers of Death (Tao Te Ching 50)
title.zh: 出生入死，十有三（道德經第五十章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 50

summary.en: Men come forth and live; they enter again and die. Of every ten, three are ministers of life and three of death; three in every ten whose aim is to live but whose movements tend to the land of death — while he who is skilful in managing his life travels without having to shun rhinoceros or tiger, for there is in him no place of death.
summary.zh: 出生入死。生之徒十有三，死之徒十有三——陸行不遇兕虎，入軍不被甲兵；兕無所投其角，虎無所措其爪，兵無所容其刃。夫何故？以其無死地。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; the 'no place of death' doctrine grounds later invulnerability claims. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: 1. Men come forth and live; they enter (again) and die. 2. Of every ten three are ministers of life (to themselves); and three are ministers of death. 3. There are also three in every ten whose aim is to live, but whose movements tend to the land (or place) of death. And for what reason? Because of their excessive endeavours to perpetuate life.

4. But I have heard that he who is skilful in managing the life entrusted to him for a time travels on the land without having to shun rhinoceros or tiger, and enters a host without having to avoid buff coat or sharp weapon. The rhinoceros finds no place in him into which to thrust its horn, nor the tiger a place in which to fix its claws, nor the weapon a place to admit its point. And for what reason? Because there is in him no place of death.

title.en: The Mother of All Under the Sky (Tao Te Ching 52)
title.zh: 天下有母，可以為天下母（道德經第五十二章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 52

summary.en: The Tao which originated all under the sky is to be considered as the mother of them all; when one knows that he is his mother's child, and proceeds to guard the qualities of the mother that belong to him, to the end of his life he will be free from all peril.
summary.zh: 天下有母，以為天下母；既得其母，以知其子——沒身不殆。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. (The Tao) which originated all under the sky is to be considered as the mother of them all. 2. When the mother is found, we know what her children should be. When one knows that he is his mother's child, and proceeds to guard (the qualities of) the mother that belong to him, to the end of his life he will be free from all peril.

3. Let him keep his mouth closed, and shut up the portals (of his nostrils), and all his life he will be exempt from laborious exertion. Let him keep his mouth open, and (spend his breath) in the promotion of his affairs, and all his life there will be no safety for him. 4. The perception of what is small is (the secret of) clear-sightedness; the guarding of what is soft and tender is (the secret of) strength.

title.en: Nothing Softer Than Water Attacks the Strong (Tao Te Ching 78)
title.zh: 天下莫柔弱於水（道德經第七十八章）

region.en: The pass of Yin Hsi (symbolic pin: Hangu Pass, Lingbao, Henan, China)
region.zh: 函谷關（象徵定位：河南靈寶）

texts.period: Tao Te Ching, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Legge, 1891)

source.work: The Tao Teh King, trans. James Legge (SBE 39), ch. 78

summary.en: There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it — he who accepts his state's reproach is hailed therefore its altars' lord; words that are strictly true seem to be paradoxical.
summary.zh: 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者莫之能勝——受國之垢，是為社稷主；受國不祥，是為天下王。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition. Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: 1. There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it;--for there is nothing (so effectual) for which it can be changed.

2. Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice. 3. Therefore a sage has said, 'He who accepts his state's reproach, Is hailed therefore its altars' lord; To him who bears men's direful woes They all the name of King accord.' 4. Words that are strictly true seem to be paradoxical.
